paras: The lynching of Lige Daniels took place on August 2, 1920, at Center, Texas, when a mob of more than a thousand men stormed the county jail and hanged Daniels, a Black man charged with murdering a white woman, from a tree in the courthouse yard. It followed the officers' announcement of his confession and came although the governor's office had ordered a cavalry company to protect him. The NAACP protested to Governor W. P. Hobby, counting it the eighth Texas lynching of the year, and a Black weekly reported that the sheriff gave the mob the keys.

According to the Associated Press, Mrs. Maggie Hall, wife of a farmer near Center, was found unconscious near her home on a Thursday night with her skull crushed, and died the next day. Daniels, suspected "from alleged threats previously made," was charged with her murder. Officers announced that he had confessed to the grand jury and to the district attorney, J. R. Anderson, a statement the AP qualified with "it was said." The Baltimore Afro-American reported talk of lynching around the courthouse since the arrest.

On the afternoon of Monday, August 2, the mob battered down the jail's steel doors, wrecked the steel cell and took Daniels out. The Afro-American described 1,500 whites armed with crowbars, sledges and tree trunks, and called the victim Elijah Daniels. Daniels was hanged from an oak limb in the courthouse yard, after which the crowd dispersed and the town "resumed its normal appearance."

Captain W. A. Bridges of Company L, Seventh Cavalry, had wire orders from Austin to protect the prisoner, but according to the AP he could not find his men in time. Black papers told it differently: the Afro-American said the public announcement of the order spurred the mob to act at once, and the Chicago Whip reported that the sheriff was said to have handed the keys to the mob's leaders and that troopers allegedly took part. Earlier that day a message from San Augustine said that if Daniels were not executed, a delegation from that county would come "to attend to the matter."

On August 3 District Judge Spottiswood Sanders instructed the grand jury to return bills against everyone connected with the lynching. No report of an inquest, indictments or a trial appears in the coverage. The same day the NAACP, in a telegram signed by James W. Johnson, reminded Hobby that he had said after two July 6 lynchings that Texas could handle its own affairs, and asked, "Is this the way in which Texas handles her own affairs?"

The AP story ran on August 3 from Washington to Montana, and reprints continued to August 6; white follow-ups were one-line briefs on the judge's charge. White headlines stressed force and the alleged crime: the Evening Star's "Mob Smashes Into Jail, Seizes and Hangs Negro" ran over "Follows Brutal Assault on White Woman. Confession Reported," and the Daily Kennebec Journal's "Negro Murderer Lynched by Mob" treated the charge as settled. A Shreveport dispatch in the Chattanooga News ran as "Louisiana Mob Lynches Negro," and the Prescott Weekly Journal-Miner headlined "Neighbor County Sends Offer To Aid Mob."

Black weeklies, writing from August 6 to September 2, pressed what the wire left out. The Cleveland Advocate, under "Gulf State Adds Victim to Score of Mob Injustice," wrote that "as customary down in this section" the mob announced a "confession" to justify itself, noted the lynchers wore no masks in daylight, and predicted a verdict of death "at the hands of unknown parties." The Chicago Whip's "Sheriff Gives Jail Keys to Mob" called the lynchers "representative citizens," and the Washington Bee printed the NAACP telegram under "Says Texas Government Completely Breaks Down." Briefs in the Tulsa Star ("Same Old Thing") and the Omaha Monitor repeated the wire facts.

Most reports dated the lynching Monday, August 2, but one reprint carried an August 1 dateline, the Omaha Monitor gave "Monday, August 1," and the Tulsa Star said "last Saturday" and called the charge assault rather than murder. The Whip's report that the sheriff gave up the keys, attributed only to what was "said," differs from the same-day AP account of the mob battering its way into the cell.

reader.title: Lynching of Lige Daniels
bases: A crowd of a thousand or more took Daniels from the county jail and hanged him in the courthouse yard (A3, A7, A22).

A mob of over a thousand men took Daniels, who was charged with murder, from jail and hanged him without trial while a grand jury was in session (A3, A7); the killing followed the officers' announcement of his confession (A7, A25).

The AP account (A3, A7), a separate Shreveport dispatch (A1), and independent Black-press accounts (A22, A28) agree that a large mob took Daniels from the Center jail and hanged him in the courthouse yard.

accounts.gist: A mob of over a thousand men battered into the jail, wrecked the steel cell and hanged Daniels after officers announced his confession; the cavalry captain could not find his men.

accounts.label: Shreveport dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of a thousand or more stormed the Center jail and hanged Daniels, 'said to have confessed'; the governor's message to Capt. Bridges came too late.

accounts.label: Afro-American correspondent
accounts.gist: Fifteen hundred whites with crowbars, sledges and tree trunks broke in; lynching talk had gone on since the arrest, and the public announcement of the troop order spurred the mob to act at once.

accounts.label: Chicago Whip
accounts.gist: The sheriff was said to have handed the cage keys to the mob's leaders, and the troopers were alleged to have been among the lynchers.

accounts.label: NAACP telegram
accounts.gist: The failure to find the cavalry company showed a breakdown of Texas government; the federal government must intervene.

framing.detail: Most white papers ran the AP story under headlines such as 'Mob Smashes Into Jail, Seizes and Hangs Negro ... Follows Brutal Assault on White Woman. Confession Reported.'
The Kennebec Journal's headline 'Negro Murderer Lynched by Mob' presented the charge as fact.
The Weekly Journal-Miner headlined the San Augustine message 'Neighbor County Sends Offer To Aid Mob.'
The Cleveland Advocate called the confession a customary mob justification and predicted an 'unknown parties' verdict.
The Chicago Whip headlined 'Sheriff Gives Jail Keys to Mob' and called the lynchers 'representative citizens' in quotation marks.
The Washington Bee ran the NAACP telegram under 'Says Texas Government Completely Breaks Down.'
